Purpose: learn how phishing attacks operate so you can detect and defend against them. The examples are intentionally benign, use dummy data, and do not target any real systems or credentials. 1) Anatomy of a phishing attack (explanation) - Lure: an attacker sends a message (email, SMS, social media) that convinces the recipient to act. This often includes urgency, a plausible sender, and a link or attachment. - Landing page / credential capture: the link points to a fake website crafted to look like a legitimate service (bank, email provider). When the victim enters credentials, the attacker captures them. - Delivery and obfuscation: attackers use lookalike domains, URL shorteners, spoofed display names, or embedded images to avoid detection. - Exfiltration and use: captured credentials are stored or sent to the attacker, who then uses them to access accounts. 2) Safe, reproducible local demonstration (HTML + simple server) This demonstration shows how a fake login page captures input locally for learning. It uses a basic HTML form and a local HTTP server that logs submitted form data. Run this only on your own machine, with dummy usernames/passwords, and never against real services or people. Files: - phishing_demo/index.html - phishing_demo/server.py a) index.html (a simple fake login page) Save this as phishing_demo/index.html Example Bank - Sign In

b) server.py (simple Python server to serve the page and log submissions) Save this as phishing_demo/server.py #!/usr/bin/env python3 from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler import urllib.parse import io HOST = '127.0.0.1' PORT = 8000 class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): if self.path == '/' or self.path.startswith('/index.html'): try: with open('index.html', 'rb') as f: content = f.read() self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html; charset=utf-8') self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(content))) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(content) except FileNotFoundError: self.send_error(404, 'Not found') else: self.send_error(404, 'Not found') def do_POST(self): if self.path == '/capture': length = int(self.headers.get('Content-Length', 0)) body = self.rfile.read(length) parsed = urllib.parse.parse_qs(body.decode('utf-8')) # Log captured fields to a local file (for study only) with open('captured_log.txt', 'a') as log: log.write('--- Submission ---\n') for k, v in parsed.items(): log.write(f'{k}: {v}\n') # Respond with a benign “error” to simulate a site behavior response = io.BytesIO() response.write(b'

') resp = response.getvalue() self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html; charset=utf-8') self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(resp))) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(resp) else: self.send_error(404, 'Not found') def run(): print(f'Serving on http://{HOST}:{PORT}/ — press Ctrl-C to stop') httpd = HTTPServer((HOST, PORT), Handler) try: httpd.serve_forever() except KeyboardInterrupt: httpd.server_close() print('Stopped.') if __name__ == '__main__': run() 3) How to run the demo safely - Create a new folder phishing_demo, place index.html and server.py inside. - In a terminal, cd into that folder and run: python3 server.py - Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in your browser. The server will write captured_log.txt in the same folder with the submitted fields. - Inspect captured_log.txt to see how credentials would be collected. 4) Detection and mitigation advice (practical, actionable) - Verify URLs: check the full URL, not just the page title or logo. Legitimate banks use their official domain and HTTPS with valid certificates. - Look for HTTPS and valid certificates: padlocks alone aren't sufficient, but absence of HTTPS is a strong red flag. - Sender scrutiny: examine email headers and sender addresses. Phishing often uses lookalike domains (exa111e.com vs example.com). - Hover links: hover over links to see the actual target before clicking. - Multi-factor authentication (MFA): enable MFA on accounts so stolen passwords are insufficient. - Anti-phishing tools: use browser phishing protection, email filters, and security extensions. - Education and drills: run simulated phishing tests for employees and teach common red flags. - Report: report suspected phishing to the service being impersonated and to your email provider. 5) Further safe experiments - Create variants of the demo that show how slight URL changes or copy variations affect detection. - Build scripts that parse server logs to analyze common credentials submitted in tests (dummy data only). - Test browser warnings by loading pages with invalid/self-signed certificates in a controlled environment.
